questions.q: You've split your Claude Code CI reviews into security, business-logic, and API-design passes. Each pass now needs to reach production quality. What most improves each pass individually?
options: Reuse the same generic few-shot examples across all three passes so that findings stay consistently formatted and comparable
Run each pass twice with different phrasings and take the union of findings, so anything either run surfaced reaches the report
Raise max_tokens on all three passes so no pass has to truncate its reasoning before reporting every finding it identified
Give each pass dedicated few-shot examples drawn from its own concern, plus explicit inclusion and exclusion boundaries for that category
questions.explain: Splitting passes pays off only when each gets concern-specific examples and explicit inclusion/exclusion boundaries, which is what defines the category for that pass. Running each pass twice and unioning is the near-miss — it can add recall, but it doubles cost and amplifies false positives without ever telling a pass what belongs in its category.

questions.q: In a Claude extraction pipeline, dates arrive in mixed forms — '3/4/26', 'March 4 2026', '2026-03-04' — breaking downstream parsing. Schema validation passes each time. Best fix?
options: Put format normalisation in the extraction prompt — always ISO 8601 YYYY-MM-DD — alongside the schema, so output is consistent at source
Add a downstream normaliser that regex-matches every date format you have observed so far and rewrites each one to a canonical form
Set the field's JSON Schema type to string with format 'date', relying on the validator to reject any value that is not ISO 8601
Retype the field as a plain string and defer all interpretation to the consumer, which already knows which locale each source uses
questions.explain: The schema types the field loosely enough that every observed form validates, so the canonical representation has to be specified in the extraction instructions — state ISO 8601 and consistency is produced at source. The format:'date' option is the strong near-miss: it names a real JSON Schema annotation, but format is advisory and commonly unenforced, and the scenario already reports validation passing on every variant.

questions.q: A status field should only ever be one of pending, shipped, delivered, cancelled, but Claude sometimes returns 'in transit' or 'on the way'. Which schema change fixes this?
options: Spell out the four allowed values in the field's description text, so the model is told plainly which statuses are acceptable here
Make the field nullable so that unrecognised statuses can be emitted as null and then filtered out before the value reaches consumers
Add a few-shot example showing each of the four statuses in use, so the model generalises from the demonstrated status vocabulary
Define the field as an enum over the four permitted values, so anything outside that set is structurally invalid rather than merely discouraged
questions.explain: An enum constrains the field to a fixed value set at the schema level, making out-of-set values invalid rather than just disfavoured. The few-shot option is the tempting near-miss — examples do steer vocabulary and would reduce 'in transit', but they remain guidance, so an unlisted value still validates; only the enum enforces the closed set.

questions.q: SCENARIO — Customer Support Resolution Agent. A conversation runs long and the full history no longer fits Claude's context. Which retention strategy preserves answer quality best?
options: Pair a sliding window of recent turns with a structured state object holding durable facts (order IDs, amounts, entitlements) plus key decisions
Truncate to just the most recent N messages and discard everything older, keeping the window small enough to stay well under the limit
Summarise the entire conversation into a single paragraph each time the limit approaches, and carry only that paragraph forward afterwards
Keep a sliding window and re-summarise the dropped turns into a rolling prose recap that is prepended to every new request
questions.explain: A sliding window alone silently drops facts established early; pairing it with a structured state object for durable values plus selective retention of decisions keeps the transactional details addressable while bounding token growth. The rolling prose recap is the strong near-miss — it does preserve some history, but repeated re-summarisation blurs exactly the order IDs and amounts a support agent must quote precisely.

questions.q: Why is a structured state object preferable to a prose running summary for tracking a Claude agent's accumulated facts across compaction cycles?
options: It occupies far more tokens than equivalent prose, which devotes a much larger share of the window to the agent's accumulated facts
Structured state can be validated against a schema, letting the runtime reject any compaction whose output has dropped a required field
Prose summaries must be re-summarised on every compaction cycle, whereas structured state is carried forward untouched and never needs updating
It keeps values addressable and unambiguous: fields are read, updated, and validated individually, while prose blurs specifics on re-summarisation
questions.explain: Structured fields stay individually readable, updatable, and verifiable, so specific values survive repeated compaction, whereas each re-summarisation of prose loses precision. Schema validation of the state is the near-miss — it is a genuine side benefit, but the core reason is addressability of the values themselves, and validation alone would not stop prose from blurring.
